title: The Gatha of Guru Arjan
hook: a short, dense poem in an old literary style (ang 1360)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sehskriti's warnings: katanch, where is mother, where is father. Your line was passing things. Who did you love well, knowing the time was a gift? Day one thousand two hundred five.

A spoonful of honey and a glass of sugar water can hold the same sweetness. One you sip for a while. The other you taste all at once, and it stays on the tongue. On Ang thirteen hundred sixty of the Guru Granth Sahib sits a short composition by Guru Arjan called the Gatha. It's the honey. Short, packed, written in an old literary style, every line carrying more than its size suggests. You don't read it quickly. You let it sit on the tongue.
screen: `HONEY AND SUGAR WATER.` → `ANG 1360.` → `LET IT SIT ON THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Gatha is often glossed as a verse or a song, and here it's the heading of the composition itself. The outline calls it short and dense, in an old literary style, and that's the doorway in. Like the Sehskriti we just read, its words carry an older, learned sound, so some Sikhs study it with someone who knows the vocabulary. Its opening lines, paraphrased, go like this. Camphor, flowers and perfume, touching the human body, become soiled. That's a startling start. We usually think of the body as the thing that needs perfume, and here the perfume is the thing that gets dirty. The image turns your expectation over. Read on, and the Gatha keeps pointing past the body's surface: the Name, the company of the holy, the Lord's praise. Each line works like a seed, small enough to hold in your palm, holding a whole tree. That's what dense means. Not difficult for its own sake, but folded, so it opens slowly. A long hymn can carry you along by its flow. A dense one asks you to stop. Read a phrase, put it down, look at it from another side. A reader can come back to a single line for days. So the Gatha teaches something by its shape. Some truths arrive in a flood of words. Others come in a spoonful, and the work is to let them dissolve.
screen: `GATHA: A VERSE, A SONG.` · `CAMPHOR AND FLOWERS, SOILED.` · `A SEED THAT HOLDS A TREE.` · `A DENSE LINE ASKS YOU TO STOP.` · then, large: `DENSE AND SHORT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it slowly. If you can find the Gatha on Ang thirteen hundred sixty, read only its first line, in Gurmukhi or in translation. Then close your eyes and let the line sit. Turn it over once. What surprises you? If you don't have it, take the paraphrase from today: camphor and flowers, touching the body, become soiled. Hold just that, and breathe with it. No need to finish the poem. One line, all the way down. The bell holds the time.
Gatha. A verse, a song; Guru Arjan's short, dense composition in an old literary style on Ang thirteen hundred sixty. Today's word.
Your line: dense and short. Today, take one short sentence someone says to you, a teacher, a friend, a child, and give it the time a long one would get. Day one thousand two hundred five.

howItsDone: The Gatha of Guru Arjan is read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib's closing sections; because of its old literary vocabulary, some Sikhs study it with a giani or a teeka, line by line.
